course.title: DevOps Basics
course.tagline: Ship software with confidence: Git, CI, Docker and cloud deploys in one practical month.

days.title: What DevOps Is
days.goal: Understand what DevOps is and why teams use it.

video.title: Docker Tutorial for Beginners [FULL COURSE in 3 Hours]

steps: Write down the old way: developers build, then throw code over the wall to operations.
Learn what DevOps changes: developers and operations work together and automate everything.
Learn the DevOps loop: plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate, monitor.
Find one company story about DevOps and write down what improved.
days.task: Write a short note: what DevOps is, in your own words, and why it matters.
days.challenge: Draw the DevOps loop on paper with one sentence for each step.

options: A way of working where development and operations teams build, test and release software together, with automation
quiz.explain: DevOps joins development and operations into one team that automates building, testing and releasing software.

options: Slow, painful releases where code sits waiting and breaks when it finally ships
quiz.explain: Without DevOps, releases are rare and risky. DevOps makes small, frequent, safe releases normal.

options: The cycle of plan, code, build, test, release, deploy, operate and monitor, repeated forever
A kind of loop in code
quiz.explain: The loop is the DevOps cycle. Each release goes around it, and monitoring feeds lessons back into planning.

days.title: Linux Command Line Refresher
days.goal: Refresh the Linux commands you will use every day in DevOps.

video.title: Kubernetes Crash Course for Absolute Beginners [NEW]

steps: Practise moving around: pwd, ls, cd and mkdir.
Practise reading files: cat, less, head and tail.
Practise searching: grep and find.
Check what is running and how much memory is free with ps and free.
days.task: Use only the terminal for one hour: no file manager, no mouse.
days.challenge: Write a cheat sheet of your ten most-used commands.

quiz.q: Why is the command line so important in DevOps?
options: Because servers have no screens, and automation runs commands, not clicks
quiz.explain: Servers are managed by commands, and automation is just commands run by a machine. The terminal is the core skill.

options: It shows the end of a file and keeps showing new lines as they appear
quiz.explain: tail -f follows a file live, which is how you watch logs as an app runs.

options: It searches inside files for lines that match a pattern
quiz.explain: grep finds lines containing a word or pattern, which is handy for reading logs.

days.title: Git Basics: Commits and Branches
days.goal: Use Git to track changes and work in branches.

video.title: DevOps Full Course 2026 | DevOps Tutorial for Beginners | DevOps Training

steps: Create a folder, run git init, and make your first commit.
Change a file, check git status, and commit the change with a clear message.
Make a branch called feature-login and switch to it.
Merge the branch back into main and check the log.
days.task: Make a small project with five commits and two branches, then merge them.
days.challenge: Write a good commit message for each change you make today.

options: A tool that tracks changes to your code so you can go back and work together
quiz.explain: Git records every change to your files. You can see history, undo mistakes and merge work from many people.

options: A separate line of work you can change without touching the main code
quiz.explain: A branch is a copy of the code you can change safely. When it works, you merge it back into main.

quiz.q: What makes a good commit message?
options: A short sentence that says what changed and why
quiz.explain: A good message explains the change in one line, so anyone reading the history understands it.

days.title: GitHub: Remote Repos and Pull Requests
days.goal: Work with GitHub: push code, open pull requests and review them.

video.title: Learning DevOps: Aws, Terraform, Ansible, Jenkins, and Docker

steps: Create a repository on GitHub and push your local project to it.
Make a change on a branch and push the branch.
Open a pull request and write a clear description of the change.
Review a pull request: read the diff and leave a comment.
days.task: Push your project to GitHub and open your first pull request.
days.challenge: Merge the pull request and delete the branch.

options: A request to merge your branch into the main code, with a review first
quiz.explain: A pull request proposes a change. Others review it, discuss it and then merge it.

options: To catch bugs, share knowledge and keep the code quality high
quiz.explain: Review catches mistakes early and spreads knowledge across the team.

quiz.q: What is the difference between git push and git pull?
options: push sends your commits to the remote, pull brings others' commits to you
quiz.explain: push uploads your work to GitHub. pull downloads work others have pushed.

days.title: Bash Scripting Basics
days.goal: Write small scripts to automate boring jobs.

video.title: Terraform explained in 15 mins | Terraform Tutorial for Beginners

steps: Write a script that prints 'Hello' and the current date.
Use a variable to store a name and print a greeting with it.
Use an if statement to check if a file exists.
Use a for loop to back up three files into a folder.
days.task: Write a backup script that copies your project folder with today's date in the name.
days.challenge: Make the script executable with chmod +x and run it with ./backup.sh.

options: A text file with commands that run one after another to automate a job
quiz.explain: A bash script is a list of commands in a file. Running it does the whole job at once.

options: Because computers do repetitive jobs faster and without mistakes
quiz.explain: A script does a boring job the same way every time, in seconds, with no typos.

options: It makes a file executable so you can run it as a program
quiz.explain: chmod +x adds the execute permission, so the system lets you run the file as a script.

days.title: What Is a CI/CD Pipeline?
days.goal: Understand continuous integration and continuous delivery.

video.title: CI/CD With GitHub Actions Tutorial: Build, Test and Deploy Automatically

steps: Learn what CI means: every change is built and tested automatically.
Learn what CD means: tested changes can be released automatically.
Draw a simple pipeline: commit, build, test, deploy.
List three things a pipeline should check: does it build, do tests pass, is it secure?
days.task: Draw a CI/CD pipeline for a small web app with four stages.
days.challenge: Write down what should happen if a test fails in the pipeline.

options: Merging code often and automatically building and testing every change
quiz.explain: CI means every change is merged, built and tested automatically, so problems are found in minutes, not weeks.

options: Keeping the code always ready to release, with deployment automated or one click away
quiz.explain: Continuous delivery means tested code is always releasable. Deployment is automated or a single click.

quiz.q: Why automate testing in a pipeline?
options: Because humans forget tests, and a pipeline runs them the same way every time
quiz.explain: A pipeline runs every test on every change, so a broken change cannot slip through.

days.title: Project 1: Version Control a Project with Git
days.goal: Put a real project under Git and GitHub with branches and pull requests.

video.title: 3-Tier Web App with Docker | Full Hands-On Tutorial

steps: Create a small web app project with at least three files.
Put it under Git with a clear first commit.
Push it to GitHub and add a README that explains the project.
Make a feature branch, add a feature, open a pull request and merge it.
days.task: Finish the project on GitHub with a README, branches and a merged pull request.
days.challenge: Show the commit history to one person and explain what each commit did.

options: A short explanation of what the project does, how to run it and how to contribute
quiz.explain: A good README tells a stranger what the project is, how to run it and how to help, in a few short sections.

options: So each feature is built safely apart from the main code
quiz.explain: Branches isolate work. A broken feature cannot break the main code until it is merged.

quiz.q: What should you do before merging a pull request?
options: Check the tests pass and at least one person reviewed it
quiz.explain: Merge only when tests are green and someone has reviewed the change.

project.title: Version Control a Project with Git
project.brief: Put a real project under Git and GitHub: a small web app with at least three files, a clear commit history, a README, a feature branch, a pull request and a merge.
checks: The project is under Git with a clear commit history.
The project is pushed to GitHub.
A README explains what the project does and how to run it.
A feature branch was created and merged through a pull request.
The pull request was reviewed before merging.
The commit messages are clear and descriptive.

days.title: Docker: Containers Explained
days.goal: Understand containers and why they changed software delivery.

video.title: What Is Ansible? | How Ansible Works? | Ansible Playbook Tutorial For Beginners | DevOps

steps: Learn what a container is: your app plus everything it needs, in one package.
Learn the difference between a container and a virtual machine.
Install Docker on your computer and check it with docker --version.
Run your first container: docker run hello-world.
days.task: Run the hello-world container and write down what happened.
days.challenge: List three problems containers solve.

options: A lightweight package with your app and its dependencies that runs the same anywhere
quiz.explain: A container bundles your app with its libraries and settings, so it runs the same on any machine.

quiz.q: How is a container different from a virtual machine?
options: A container shares the host's operating system, so it is smaller and starts in seconds
quiz.explain: A VM carries a whole operating system. A container shares the host OS, so it is light and fast to start.

options: 'It works on my machine': the app runs the same everywhere because its environment travels with it
quiz.explain: Containers carry their environment with them, so an app that works on your laptop works on the server too.

days.title: Docker Images and Dockerfiles
days.goal: Build your own Docker image with a Dockerfile.

video.title: Deploy a 3-Tier App on AWS EC2: React, Node.js, MySQL

steps: Write a Dockerfile for a simple web app: FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, CMD.
Build the image with docker build -t my-app .
Run a container from your image and open it in a browser.
Check the image layers with docker history.
days.task: Build a Docker image of a small web page and run it on your computer.
days.challenge: Change the page, rebuild the image and run it again.

options: A text file with instructions for building a Docker image
quiz.explain: A Dockerfile lists the steps to build an image: start from a base, copy files, install things, set the startup command.

options: A frozen template of an app and its environment, used to start containers
quiz.explain: An image is a snapshot. A container is a running copy of an image.

options: It reads a Dockerfile and creates an image
quiz.explain: docker build follows the Dockerfile's instructions and packs the result into an image.

days.title: Docker Compose: Multi-Container Apps
days.goal: Run a whole app with several containers using Docker Compose.

video.title: Docker Tutorial for Beginners - A Full DevOps Course on How to Run Applications in Containers

steps: Write a docker-compose.yml with a web service and a database service.
Start both with docker compose up.
Check the web app can talk to the database.
Stop everything with docker compose down.
days.task: Build a two-container app: a web page and a database, running with one command.
days.challenge: Add a third service: a cache or a worker.

options: A tool that runs several containers together from one YAML file
quiz.explain: Compose describes your whole app's containers in one file and starts them together with one command.

quiz.q: What is a service in Compose?
options: One container in your app, like web or db, defined in the YAML file
quiz.explain: A service is one part of your app, like the web server or the database, that Compose runs as a container.

quiz.q: Why use Compose instead of many docker run commands?
options: Because one file describes the whole app, so anyone can start it with one command
quiz.explain: One Compose file is the recipe for the whole app. Anyone can run it with a single command.

days.title: Docker Volumes and Networks
days.goal: Keep data safe with volumes and connect containers with networks.

video.title: Learn Docker by Building a Node / Express App

steps: Create a volume and store database data in it.
Stop and remove the container, then start a new one with the same volume and check the data is still there.
Create a network and put two containers on it so they can talk by name.
List your volumes and networks with docker volume ls and docker network ls.
days.task: Run a database in a container with a volume, add data, restart the container and check the data survived.
days.challenge: Connect a web container to a database container by name.

options: Storage that lives outside a container, so data survives when the container is deleted
quiz.explain: A volume is persistent storage. Data in a volume stays even when the container is removed.

options: Because a container's own files disappear when it is deleted, so data needs a home outside it
quiz.explain: Containers are disposable. Without a volume, your database would vanish with the container.

options: A virtual network that lets containers talk to each other by name
quiz.explain: A network connects containers so they can reach each other by service name, like db or web.

days.title: Kubernetes: Pods and Deployments
days.goal: Understand Kubernetes and run your first pod.

video.title: Docker Tutorial for Beginners [FULL COURSE in 3 Hours]

steps: Learn what Kubernetes does: it runs and manages many containers for you.
Learn the main pieces: pod, deployment, service and node.
Install minikube or kind and start a local cluster.
Deploy a simple app with kubectl apply and check it with kubectl get pods.
days.task: Start a local Kubernetes cluster and deploy a simple web app.
days.challenge: Check the pods are running and open the app in a browser.

options: A system that runs, scales and heals containers across many machines
quiz.explain: Kubernetes manages containers for you: it places them, restarts them when they fail and scales them up or down.

options: The smallest unit in Kubernetes: one or more containers that run together
quiz.explain: A pod is a group of containers that share a network and storage. It is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs.

options: A recipe that says how many copies of your app should run, and keeps that many alive
quiz.explain: A deployment manages pods. You say 'run three copies', and Kubernetes keeps three running, replacing any that die.

days.title: Kubernetes Services and Ingress
days.goal: Expose your app to the world with services and ingress.

video.title: Kubernetes Crash Course for Absolute Beginners [NEW]

steps: Learn what a service does: it gives your pods a stable address.
Create a service for your app and check you can reach it.
Learn what ingress does: it routes web traffic to the right service.
Add an ingress rule that sends traffic to your app.
days.task: Expose your app with a service and open it in a browser.
days.challenge: Add a second app and route traffic to each by path.

options: A stable address in front of your pods, so traffic reaches them even as pods change
quiz.explain: Pods come and go. A service gives them one stable address that always points at the live pods.

options: A rule that routes incoming web traffic to the right service
quiz.explain: Ingress is the front door. It reads the URL and sends each request to the right service.

quiz.q: Why do pods need a service?
options: Because pods get new addresses when they restart, so clients need a stable address
quiz.explain: Pods are temporary and their addresses change. A service hides that churn behind one fixed address.

days.title: Project 2: Containerise and Deploy a 3-Tier App
days.goal: Containerise a 3-tier app and run it with Docker Compose and Kubernetes.

video.title: DevOps Full Course 2026 | DevOps Tutorial for Beginners | DevOps Training

steps: Take a simple 3-tier app: frontend, backend and database.
Write a Dockerfile for the frontend and one for the backend.
Run the whole app with Docker Compose.
Deploy the same app to your local Kubernetes cluster.
days.task: Finish the containerised 3-tier app and open it in a browser.
days.challenge: Write down the commands to start and stop the whole app.

options: An app split into three layers: frontend, backend and database
quiz.explain: A 3-tier app has three layers: the user interface, the logic, and the data. Each layer can change and scale on its own.

options: So each layer can be built, tested and scaled on its own
quiz.explain: Separate containers let you update the frontend without touching the database, and scale each layer as needed.

options: You can open it in a browser and use it end to end
quiz.explain: The proof is a working app: open it, click through it, and see data flow from the frontend to the database and back.

project.title: Containerise and Deploy a 3-Tier App
project.brief: Containerise a 3-tier app (frontend, backend, database) with Dockerfiles, run it with Docker Compose, and deploy the same app to a local Kubernetes cluster.
checks: A Dockerfile exists for the frontend and the backend.
The app runs with docker compose up.
The database keeps its data in a volume.
The app is deployed to a local Kubernetes cluster.
The app works end to end in a browser.
You can start and stop the whole app with documented commands.

days.title: CI with GitHub Actions
days.goal: Build a pipeline that tests your code on every push.

video.title: Learning DevOps: Aws, Terraform, Ansible, Jenkins, and Docker

steps: Create a .github/workflows folder in your project.
Write a workflow that runs on every push: check out the code, install dependencies, run tests.
Push the workflow and watch it run in the Actions tab.
Make a test fail on purpose and watch the pipeline go red.
days.task: Add a GitHub Actions workflow to your project that runs tests on every push.
days.challenge: Fix the failing test and watch the pipeline go green.

options: A CI/CD service built into GitHub that runs workflows when things happen in your repo
quiz.explain: GitHub Actions runs automated jobs when you push, open a pull request or on a schedule.

options: A YAML file that describes the jobs and steps to run
quiz.explain: A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows. It says when to run and what steps to do.

quiz.q: Why run tests on every push?
options: So a broken change is caught in minutes, before it reaches anyone else
quiz.explain: Testing every push catches breakage early, when it is cheap and easy to fix.

days.title: Automated Testing in the Pipeline
days.goal: Add unit tests and a test stage to your pipeline.

video.title: Terraform explained in 15 mins | Terraform Tutorial for Beginners

steps: Write three unit tests for a small function in your project.
Run the tests locally and check they pass.
Add a test step to your GitHub Actions workflow.
Push and watch the pipeline run your tests.
days.task: Write tests for your project and add them to the pipeline.
days.challenge: Add a test that fails if the output is wrong, and watch the pipeline catch it.

options: A test of the whole app
A test of one small function or piece of logic on its own
quiz.explain: A unit test checks one function in isolation, like a date formatter or a total calculator.

quiz.q: Why run tests in the pipeline, not just on your laptop?
options: Because the pipeline runs them the same way every time, on a clean machine
quiz.explain: Your laptop may have different versions or files. The pipeline tests on a clean machine, so results are trustworthy.

quiz.q: What should the pipeline do when a test fails?
options: Stop and mark the build red, so the broken change is not released
quiz.explain: A failed test stops the pipeline. The broken change must be fixed before it can move forward.

days.title: Terraform Basics
days.goal: Describe infrastructure as code with Terraform.

video.title: CI/CD With GitHub Actions Tutorial: Build, Test and Deploy Automatically

steps: Learn what infrastructure as code means: your servers and buckets written in files.
Install Terraform and check it with terraform --version.
Write a file that creates a simple resource, like a local file or an S3 bucket.
Run terraform plan to see what it would do, without doing it.
days.task: Write a Terraform file that creates an S3 bucket and run terraform plan.
days.challenge: Write down what terraform plan showed you.

options: A tool that creates and manages cloud resources from files you write
quiz.explain: Terraform reads files that describe your infrastructure and makes the real cloud match them.

options: Writing your servers, networks and buckets as files you can version and repeat
quiz.explain: Infrastructure as code means your cloud setup lives in files. You can review it, version it and recreate it exactly.

options: It shows what Terraform would change, without changing anything
quiz.explain: plan previews the changes. You read it first, then apply only when it looks right.

days.title: Terraform: Real Infrastructure
days.goal: Build real cloud infrastructure with Terraform and manage its state.

video.title: 3-Tier Web App with Docker | Full Hands-On Tutorial

steps: Write Terraform files for a VPC, a subnet and a security group.
Run terraform apply and check the resources appear in the console.
Change one value, run apply again and watch Terraform update only that thing.
Destroy the resources with terraform destroy when you are done.
days.task: Build a small VPC with Terraform, check it in the console, then destroy it.
days.challenge: Write down what terraform state is and why it matters.

options: A file that records what Terraform created, so it knows what exists
quiz.explain: State is Terraform's memory. It records what it built, so it can update or delete exactly those resources.

options: Without it, Terraform cannot tell what it owns or what to change
quiz.explain: State lets Terraform compare your files with reality and change only what differs.

options: So you stop paying for things you no longer need
quiz.explain: Cloud resources cost money while they exist. Destroying test resources stops the bill.

days.title: Ansible: Configuration Management
days.goal: Configure servers automatically with Ansible playbooks.

video.title: What Is Ansible? | How Ansible Works? | Ansible Playbook Tutorial For Beginners | DevOps

steps: Learn what Ansible does: it configures servers by running tasks from a playbook.
Install Ansible and write an inventory file with your server's address.
Write a playbook that installs a web server and starts it.
Run the playbook and check the web server is running.
days.task: Write an Ansible playbook that installs and starts a web server on your VM.
days.challenge: Run the playbook twice and notice the second run changes nothing.

options: A tool that configures servers by running tasks from playbooks, over SSH
quiz.explain: Ansible automates server setup. You describe the desired state in a playbook, and Ansible makes it so.

options: A YAML file that lists the tasks Ansible should run on your servers
quiz.explain: A playbook is a list of tasks in YAML, like 'install nginx' and 'start the service'.

options: Running a playbook twice gives the same result as running it once
quiz.explain: Idempotent means safe to repeat. Ansible only changes what is different, so a second run does nothing.

days.title: Monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana
days.goal: Watch your app's health with metrics and dashboards.

video.title: Deploy a 3-Tier App on AWS EC2: React, Node.js, MySQL

steps: Learn what a metric is: a number that shows how a system is doing.
Run Prometheus in a container and point it at your app.
Run Grafana and connect it to Prometheus.
Build a dashboard with CPU, memory and request graphs.
days.task: Build a Grafana dashboard with three graphs for your app.
days.challenge: Set an alert for when CPU goes above 80%.

options: A monitoring system that collects numbers (metrics) from your apps and servers
quiz.explain: Prometheus scrapes metrics from your services and stores them so you can ask questions about them.

options: A tool that draws dashboards and alerts from data sources like Prometheus
quiz.explain: Grafana turns metrics into charts and dashboards, and can alert you when something is wrong.

options: So you know when it is slow or broken, often before users tell you
quiz.explain: Monitoring tells you what is happening. Without it, you only learn about problems from angry users.

days.title: Project 3: Full CI/CD Pipeline to the Cloud
days.goal: Build a complete pipeline: test, build, push an image and deploy to the cloud.

video.title: Docker Tutorial for Beginners - A Full DevOps Course on How to Run Applications in Containers

steps: Take your 3-tier app and add a GitHub Actions workflow.
Make the pipeline run tests, build Docker images and push them to a registry.
Add a deploy step that updates your Kubernetes cluster or EC2 server.
Push a change and watch it flow through the pipeline to the live app.
days.task: Finish the pipeline and deploy a change through it to the live app.
days.challenge: Write down each stage of your pipeline and what it does.

options: It tests, builds, ships and deploys code automatically, with checks at each stage
quiz.explain: A complete pipeline takes code from commit to live, testing and checking it at every stage, with no manual steps in between.

quiz.q: Why push images to a registry?
options: So the deploy step can pull the exact tested image, instead of rebuilding it
quiz.explain: A registry stores the tested image. The deploy step pulls that exact image, so what you tested is what you ship.

quiz.q: How do you know the pipeline worked?
options: The live app shows your change, and every stage in the pipeline is green
quiz.explain: Green stages plus the change visible in the live app prove the pipeline works end to end.

project.title: Full CI/CD Pipeline to the Cloud
project.brief: Build a complete CI/CD pipeline for your 3-tier app: GitHub Actions runs tests, builds Docker images, pushes them to a registry, and deploys to the cloud. Push a change and watch it flow through the pipeline to the live app.
checks: A GitHub Actions workflow exists in the project.
The pipeline runs tests on every push.
The pipeline builds Docker images and pushes them to a registry.
A deploy step updates the live app.
A pushed change appears in the live app.
Every stage of the pipeline is green.

days.title: Jenkins Basics
days.goal: Meet Jenkins, the classic CI/CD server, and run a simple job.

video.title: Learn Docker by Building a Node / Express App

steps: Learn what Jenkins is: a server that runs your pipelines.
Run Jenkins in a Docker container on your computer.
Create a job that checks out your code and runs its tests.
Trigger the job by hand and read the build log.
days.task: Run Jenkins in Docker and create a job that tests your project.
days.challenge: Write down the difference between Jenkins and GitHub Actions.

options: An open-source automation server that runs builds, tests and deployments
quiz.explain: Jenkins is a server that runs your pipelines. You define jobs, and Jenkins runs them on triggers or schedules.

quiz.q: How is Jenkins different from GitHub Actions?
options: Jenkins is a server you run yourself, Actions is built into GitHub
quiz.explain: Jenkins runs on your own server, which you control fully. GitHub Actions runs on GitHub's servers.

options: A file in your repo that defines the pipeline as code
quiz.explain: A Jenkinsfile is a pipeline written as code in your repository, so it is versioned with your project.

days.title: Deployment Strategies: Blue-Green and Rolling
days.goal: Release safely with blue-green and rolling deployments.

video.title: Docker Tutorial for Beginners [FULL COURSE in 3 Hours]

steps: Learn blue-green: run two copies, switch traffic to the new one, keep the old one ready.
Learn rolling: replace servers one by one so the app never stops.
Learn canary: send a small share of users to the new version first.
Pick a strategy for your app and write down why.
days.task: Do a rolling update of your app in Kubernetes and watch it stay available.
days.challenge: Write down when you would pick blue-green over rolling.

options: Two identical environments: switch traffic from blue (old) to green (new), and switch back if it fails
quiz.explain: Blue-green keeps two copies. You switch traffic to the new one, and if it breaks, you switch back in seconds.

options: Replacing servers one by one so the app stays up during the release
quiz.explain: A rolling update replaces instances gradually. Users never see downtime, because some old copies keep serving.

options: Sending a small share of users to the new version first to check it is safe
quiz.explain: A canary release sends a few users to the new version. If it works, you roll it out to everyone.

days.title: Logging and Debugging in Production
days.goal: Find problems in a live app using logs.

video.title: Kubernetes Crash Course for Absolute Beginners [NEW]

steps: Learn what good logs look like: time, level, message and context.
Read the logs of your running containers with docker logs.
Read the logs of a pod with kubectl logs.
Find one error in the logs and fix the cause.
days.task: Find and fix one real error in your app's logs.
days.challenge: Add a log line to your app that shows when a request starts and ends.

quiz.q: What makes a good log line?
options: It has a time, a level (info, warning, error), a clear message and useful context
quiz.explain: A good log line tells you when, how serious, what happened and which request it was about.

options: Because logs are often the only record of what went wrong
quiz.explain: When a live app breaks, logs show what happened. Without them, you are guessing.

quiz.q: What is the difference between logs and metrics?
options: Logs record events with detail, metrics are numbers over time
quiz.explain: Logs tell you what happened in detail. Metrics show trends, like how often errors happen.

days.title: Security in DevOps (DevSecOps)
days.goal: Build security into your pipeline instead of bolting it on at the end.

video.title: DevOps Full Course 2026 | DevOps Tutorial for Beginners | DevOps Training

steps: Add a step to your pipeline that scans dependencies for known problems.
Scan your Docker image for vulnerabilities.
Check that no secrets (passwords, keys) are in your code or Git history.
Fix one vulnerability the scan found.
days.task: Add a security scan to your pipeline and fix the first issue it finds.
days.challenge: Remove a secret from your code and replace it with an environment variable.

options: Building security into every stage of DevOps, instead of checking it only at the end
quiz.explain: DevSecOps means security is part of the pipeline: scans and checks run on every change, not just before release.

options: Because your app includes other people's code, and a flaw in one library can break your app
quiz.explain: Most apps are mostly libraries. A known flaw in a library is a known flaw in your app.

quiz.q: Why must secrets never live in code?
options: Because code is copied, shared and stored, so a secret in code spreads everywhere
quiz.explain: Code gets cloned, shared and archived. A secret in code is a secret that has already leaked.

days.title: Cloud Deploys: EC2 and S3
days.goal: Deploy your app to AWS with EC2 and S3.

video.title: Learning DevOps: Aws, Terraform, Ansible, Jenkins, and Docker

steps: Launch an EC2 instance and install Docker on it.
Run your containerised app on the instance.
Host your frontend files on S3 with static website hosting.
Open your app in a browser and check it works.
days.task: Deploy your app to EC2 and S3 and share the link.
days.challenge: Write down the steps to deploy again from scratch.

quiz.q: Why deploy to the cloud instead of your laptop?
options: Because a cloud server is always on and reachable by anyone
quiz.explain: Your laptop sleeps and moves. A cloud server is always on, so your app is always reachable.

quiz.q: What runs where in this deploy?
options: The frontend files sit on S3, the backend runs in containers on EC2
quiz.explain: Static files are cheap on S3. The backend needs a running server, so it goes on EC2.

quiz.q: What should you check after deploying?
options: That the site loads, the data flows, and the security group only allows what it should
quiz.explain: After deploying, check the site works, the data loads, and the security group only allows what it should.

days.title: Cost and Performance in the Cloud
days.goal: Keep cloud costs low and apps fast.

video.title: Terraform explained in 15 mins | Terraform Tutorial for Beginners

steps: Find the cost of your running resources in the AWS billing page.
Right-size an instance: pick the smallest size that still performs well.
Stop resources you are not using.
Use a CDN or caching to make your app faster without bigger servers.
days.task: Check your cloud bill and stop anything you are not using.
days.challenge: Write down three ways to cut the cost of your deployment.

options: Picking the smallest instance that still runs your app well
quiz.explain: Right-sizing means matching the server to the workload. A server that is mostly idle wastes money.

options: Because serving a saved copy is faster and cheaper than computing it again
quiz.explain: A cache stores results, so repeated requests get a fast answer without re-running the work.

quiz.q: What is the biggest beginner cost mistake?
options: Leaving servers and services running when nobody uses them
quiz.explain: Idle servers are the classic surprise bill. Turn off what you do not use.

days.title: Incident Response and On-Call Basics
days.goal: Learn what to do when production breaks.

video.title: CI/CD With GitHub Actions Tutorial: Build, Test and Deploy Automatically

steps: Learn the steps: detect, acknowledge, investigate, fix, review.
Practise reading an alert and writing a short summary of what is wrong.
Learn what a runbook is: written steps for fixing common problems.
Write a runbook for one common problem in your app.
days.task: Write a runbook for restarting your app when it stops responding.
days.challenge: Practise a fake incident: your app is down. What do you do first?

options: An event that breaks or degrades a live service
quiz.explain: An incident is when production breaks or slows down enough that users notice.

options: Written steps for fixing a known problem, so anyone on call can follow them
quiz.explain: A runbook is a recipe for fixing a common problem. It means the fix does not depend on one person's memory.

options: A review after an incident that asks what happened, why, and how to stop it happening again
quiz.explain: A postmortem looks back at an incident without blame, finds the root cause and fixes it.

days.title: DevOps Culture and Teamwork
days.goal: Learn the human side of DevOps: blameless culture and shared ownership.

video.title: 3-Tier Web App with Docker | Full Hands-On Tutorial

steps: Learn what blameless culture means: fix the system, not the person.
Learn what shared ownership means: the team owns the code and the running service.
Practise giving feedback on a teammate's change kindly and specifically.
Write down one way you will help your team when something breaks.
days.task: Write a short note on what blameless culture means to you.
days.challenge: Review a teammate's change and leave one helpful comment.

options: When something breaks, the team fixes the system instead of blaming a person
quiz.explain: Blameless culture says mistakes come from systems, not bad people. Fix the system so the mistake cannot happen again.

options: The whole team owns the code and the live service together
quiz.explain: Shared ownership means the team builds it and runs it together. No one throws code over the wall.

quiz.q: Why does culture matter in DevOps?
options: Because tools alone cannot fix a team that does not trust each other or share responsibility
quiz.explain: DevOps is mostly about people. Without trust and shared ownership, the tools do not help.

days.title: Capstone Prep: Plan Your DevOps Project
days.goal: Review everything, pick your capstone project and plan your demo.

video.title: What Is Ansible? | How Ansible Works? | Ansible Playbook Tutorial For Beginners | DevOps

steps: List the projects you built and pick the strongest one to finish.
Write a short plan: the app, the pipeline, the infrastructure and the demo.
Draw a simple diagram of your pipeline and your infrastructure.
Practise explaining your project in simple words, as if to a friend.
days.task: Write your capstone plan and a one-minute explanation of your project.
days.challenge: Show your pipeline diagram to one person and note their questions.

quiz.q: What makes a good capstone DevOps project?
options: A real app with a working pipeline, automated tests, and a live deployment
quiz.explain: A good capstone shows the full loop: code, tests, pipeline and a live app that updates when you push.

quiz.q: Why draw a diagram of your pipeline?
options: So anyone can see how code flows from commit to live at a glance
quiz.explain: A diagram shows the whole flow in one picture: stages, checks and where the code ends up.

quiz.q: What should your capstone plan include?
options: The app, the pipeline stages, the infrastructure and how you will show it
quiz.explain: A plan covers the app, the pipeline, the infrastructure and how you will present it.

capstone.title: Build a Complete DevOps Pipeline and Deploy a Live App
capstone.brief: Take a real web app and give it a complete DevOps setup: Git version control with pull requests, a CI/CD pipeline with automated tests and security scans, Docker images, Terraform infrastructure, and a live deployment on AWS that updates automatically when you push code. Present a live demo and a diagram of your pipeline.
checks: The app is under Git with a clear history and pull requests.
A CI/CD pipeline runs tests on every push.
The pipeline includes a security scan.
Docker images are built and stored in a registry.
Infrastructure is described in Terraform files.
The app is live on AWS and updates when you push.
You can present a live demo and explain the pipeline in simple words.
deliverables: A working web app with a live link.
A GitHub repository with the code and pipeline files.
A diagram of the pipeline and infrastructure.
A README.md explaining the project and how to run it.
A short demo video or screenshots showing a push flowing to the live app.
